title: Function‐Decoupled Dual‐Anion Doping via Site‐Preferential Regulation Enables High‐Performance Lithium Argyrodite Electrolytes
authors: Yaru Shi, Libin Hu, Qiuhong Li, Wenhao Fang, Zheng Zhang, Xiaoyu Liu et al.
abstract: All‐solid‐state lithium metal batteries adopting argyrodite‐type sulfide solid‐state electrolytes (SSEs) offer enhanced safety and energy density, yet face challenges in balancing ionic conductivity, air stability and interfacial compatibility. Herein, we pioneer a precursor‐directed site‐preferential dual‐anion doping strategy to address these trade‐offs. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal the oxygen precursor dictates the predominant anion occupancy: Li 2 O kinetically favors O at the 4d sites, whereas P 2 O 5 preferentially directs O to the 16e sites. Guided by this principle, Li 6 PS 4.2 O 0.4 Se 0.4 Cl (LPSOSeCl) SSEs is designed, wherein O preferentially enriches 16e sites to enhance air stability and widen the electrochemical window for high‐voltage cathode compatibility, whereas Se preferentially enriches 4d sites to compensate ionic conductivity and promote a Li 2 Se/Li 2 O‐rich interphase for dendrite suppression. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations combined with radial distribution functions (RDFs) further reveal that the Se/O co‐doping facilitates the formation of a stable Li/SSE interface, significantly inhibiting LPSOSeCl SSE reduction. The resulting LPSOSeCl SSE achieves high ionic conductivity, excellent moist air stability and remarkable critical current density (CCD) of 2.6 mA cm −2. The Li||Li symmetric cells demonstrate ultralong cycling stability over 4000 h at 0.2 mA cm −2 and LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 full cells rentain 70.7% capacity retention after 500 cycles at 0.3C.

title: Al/F Co‐Doped Sulfide Electrolyte for Durable All‐Solid‐State Lithium‐Organic Batteries
authors: Menglin Li, Shuo Xu, Weili Wang, Chenchen Wang, Weiwei Huang, Kai Zhang et al.
abstract: Carbonyl‐containing organic cathodes offer a sustainable route to high‐energy storage, but their reaction with conventional sulfide electrolytes (SEs) causes interfacial degradation in all‐solid‐state lithium‐metal batteries (ASSLMBs). Here we develop an electrolyte‐first strategy that stabilizes both carbonyl cathodes and lithium metal through dual‐site Al/F substitution of an argyrodite SE, Li 5.7 Al 0.1 P 0.9 S 4.5 Cl 1.2 F 0.3 (LPSC‐AF). Hard‐soft acid‐base theory (HSAB) guided local‐bonding reconstruction increases the basicity and hard‐base character of SE ligands, strengthens P‐S coordination and passivates reactive P‐centered sites. Consequently, the 1,2,5,6‐anthracenetetrone (ATO) adsorption energy decreases from −4.41 to −0.15 eV, suppressing interfacial acid‐base coordination, nucleophilic attack and coupled redox reactions. LPSC‐AF retains an ionic conductivity of 3.8 mS cm −1 and supports stable lithium plating/stripping for over 3000 h. ATO‐based ASSLMBs deliver 358.3 mAh g −1 with 100% initial Coulombic efficiency and retain 81% capacity after 2000 cycles at 5 C and 60°C. The approach is also applicable to C4Q cathodes, establishing HSAB‐guided SEs redesign as a route to stable all‐solid‐state lithium‐organic batteries.

title: Li–B–Mg Composite Foils With a LiB 0.88 Microrod Array Enable Ultrathin Self‐Supporting Lithium Metal Anodes
authors: Xinghao Zhang, Xiaosong Xiong, Jie Wang, Xinying Wang, Shengyao Luo, Xi Liu et al.
abstract: Ultrathin self-supporting lithium foils (USSLFs, ≤50 µm) are highly desirable for high-energy-density batteries, as eliminating current collectors enhances energy density and reduces material costs. However, the intrinsic mechanical vulnerability of metallic Li remains a critical barrier to both the fabrication and long-term cycling of USSLFs. Herein, we develop a Li-rich Li-B-Mg composite foil (LBM) through sequential melt alloying followed by post-solidification thermomechanical processing, yielding a dense and interconnected LiB0.88 microrod array with LiMg and MgB2 lithiophilic phases within the Li-rich matrix. This architecture enables large-area (>170 cm2) self-supporting foils down to 15 µm while preserving a high Li content. During cycling, the microrod array redistributes local stress and restrains deformation, preserving the internal architecture and accessibility of lithiophilic sites. These sites, in turn, favor Li accommodation within the electrode interior, suppressing surface Li accumulation and alleviating local stress concentration. This self-sustained coupling between stress regulation and lithiophilic guidance supports stable cycling for over 5000 h in symmetric cells using 50 µm LBM foils with about 10% thickness expansion, while 15 µm foils cycle for over 500 h at a depth of discharge of about 37.4%. This work advances the design of practical USSLFs for high-energy lithium metal batteries.

title: A Scalable Protrusion‐Targeted Electrolyte Enables 500 Wh Kg −1 Lithium Metal Batteries With 500‐Cycle Stability
authors: Shengkai Mo, Jiamin Yang, Zongfan Yang, Ge Zhu, Haiqing Lv, Dehua Xu et al.
abstract: The development of lithium metal batteries (LMBs) is severely impeded by limited cycle life arising from irreversible lithium dendrite growth. Herein, we design a scalable, protrusion-targeted electrolytes to achieve industrial-scale LMBs through retarding the formation of dendritic lithium embryos. The site-selective-blocking molecules preferentially adsorbs onto protrusive sites of lithium deposition, which inhibits the local lithium deposition rate to block dendrite initiation. More importantly, the abundant polar functional groups of adsorbed molecules induce directional enrichment of anions, achieving passivation repair of fresh dendritic lithium. This synergy of selective adsorption and interfacial repair effectively inhibits the self-amplifying growth of lithium dendrites, thereby mitigating continuous electrolyte consumption. An 8 Ah-level pouch cell with 500 Wh kg-1 delivers an impressive capacity retention of over 80% after 525 cycles. Furthermore, we show large-scale production of electrolytes for preparing industrial-scale LMBs. This design offers a viable approach for long-life LMBs at an industry compatible scale.

title: Covalently Integrated MXene–Fluorinated Polymer Electrolytes for 714 Wh Kg −1 Lithium–Metal Batteries
authors: Xingchen Song, Nuo Xu, Po Bian, Yuhu Li, Genglin Lou, Guolin Sun et al.
abstract: Polymer electrolytes are promising for high-energy and safe lithium-metal batteries yet limited by inadequate mechanical integrity, sluggish Li+ transport, and unstable electrode-electrolyte interfaces. Here, we report a covalently integrated MXene-fluorinated gel polymer electrolyte (MF-GPE) through in situ polymerization. Acrylate-grafted MXene nanosheets act as chemically anchored crosslinkers within a fluorinated polymer network, distinguishing from conventional physically blended composites. The covalent framework not only mechanically reinforces the polymer matrix but also regulates Li+ solvation structure and lowers the activation energy for Li+ transport. Consequently, the MF-GPE enables uniform lithium deposition and constructs robust, inorganic-rich interphases on both lithium-metal anodes and high-voltage cathodes. It delivers an ionic conductivity of 3.3 mS cm-1 at 25°C and supports stable cycling of LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2, LiCoO2 and LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4 cathodes at cut-off voltages up to 4.9 V. Notably, a MF-GPE based Li||LiCoO2 pouch cell achieves cell-level energy densities of 713.9 Wh kg-1 at 4.8 V and 605.2 Wh kg-1 at 4.6 V, maintaining stable operation over 60 cycles, while 18650 cylindrical cells operate stably for 500 cycles. Ah-class pouch cells demonstrate outstanding safety under nail-penetration and overcharge tests. These findings establish covalent MXene-polymer integration to couple ion solvation structure and interphase stabilization for high-energy, abuse-tolerant lithium-metal batteries.

title: Fabrication of Tri‐Phase Lithium Alloy in Seconds via an Implosion‐Popcorn Reaction Toward Stable Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Xinqi Wei, Gaofeng Du, Haoyue Liang, Mingyang Zhong, Cheng Zeng, Yanpeng Guo et al.
abstract: Introducing non‐lithium components to fabricate lithium‐based alloy anodes has emerged as a paramount strategy to enhance the processability and stability of lithium metal batteries. However, conventional fabrication suffers from the sluggish wetting kinetics of lithium with non‐lithium components, inducing severe phase heterogeneity and component agglomeration. Herein, we report an ultrafast, spontaneous implosion‐popcorn reaction that explosively disintegrates centimeter‐scale precursor ingots into ultra‐fine particles within seconds, yielding a uniformly dispersed tri‐phase alloy with an interpenetrating network of Fe, Li 3 P, and Li. The as‐obtained lithium alloy exhibits a significantly enhanced Young's modulus and can be processed into different forms, including coatable slurries, self‐standing foils, and active powders. This fabrication method shifts from traditional passive alloying to an active, highly efficient, and homogenous approach. When used as an anode, the homogeneous Li/Fe/Li 3 P architecture facilitates interfacial Li‐ion transfer and regulates initial Li nucleation, thereby promoting dense and uniform Li growth and enabling a cycling lifespan of over 3000 h, together with improved full‐cell stability.

title: Constructing Low‐Friction Ion Transport Pathways in Crosslinked Polymer Electrolyte for Practical Quasi‐Solid‐State Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Shuaishuai Yan, Hao Liu, Wenhui Hou, Yang Lu, Zhang Jia, Xiao Ma et al.
abstract: Quasi-solid-state polymer electrolytes are promising candidates for lithium metal batteries (LMBs) with high energy density, but still suffer from sacrificed ionic conductivity caused by electrolyte solidification. Here, by tuning monomer structures with different Li+-affinity, we investigate the decisive role of the segmental solvation ability of the polymer matrix in cation transport. Owing to the overly strong affinity for cations, conventional ether segments significantly decrease the Li+ relaxation rate, and the resulting "sticky" polymer chains impede Li+ migration. In contrast, the weakly coordinating segments such as fluorinated ether could effectively minimize coupling with Li+ ions, thereby constructing "low-friction" cation transport pathways in crosslinked polymer electrolytes, as reflected by the nearly unchanged Li+ relaxation kinetics and high ionic conductivity. Therefore, the industrial Li metal pouch cells achieve excellent comprehensive electrochemical performance under harsh lean-electrolyte conditions, with electrolyte dosage even as low as 1.3 g Ah-1. The 2 Ah NCM811/Li cell exhibits an extended lifespan beyond 520 cycles and maintains stable operation across a wide temperature range from -50°C to +90°C. The 8.7 Ah NCM955/Li cell delivers 550 Wh kg-1 energy density and demonstrates impressive cycling stability over 260 cycles. This work could inspire fundamental understanding and further development toward practical LMBs.

title: Competitive Solvation Structure in a Deep Eutectic Electrolyte Enables High‐Voltage LiCoO 2 ‐Based Pouch Cells With 5000‐Cycle Stability
authors: Huijie Tian, Erlei Zhang, Jialin Wang, Qing Li, Yunyun Lei, Hao Wu et al.
abstract: Anion‐rich solvation structures improve interfacial stability but often impede Li + desolvation, limiting fast‐charging and low‐temperature performance in high‐voltage lithium metal batteries. Unlike conventional high‐concentration or weakly solvating electrolytes, we propose a deep eutectic electrolyte (DEE) using succinonitrile (SN) and dimethyl sulfone (MSM) with competitive coordination capability. This design shifts the Li + solvation from aggregate clusters (AGGs) to a balanced AGGs/contact ion pairs (CIPs) distribution, which lowers the Li + desolvation energy barrier, enhances the transport kinetics, and endows the DEE with an ionic conductivity of 3.87 mS cm −1 and a Li + transference number of 0.81. MSM moderates excessive SN coordination, suppressing parasitic reactions on the anode, thereby enabling stable Li plating/stripping for 6800 h. A lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI)/lithium difluoro(oxalato)borate (LiDFOB) dual‐salt system further optimizes interfacial chemistry, yielding a bilayer solid electrolyte interphase comprising an inorganic‐rich inner layer and a flexible organic outer layer. LiCoO 2 ||Li cells retain 97.1% capacity after 1000 cycles at 5C (3.0–4.5 V) and operate stably at −10°C. A 3.0 Ah LiCoO 2 ||Li pouch cell further delivers a high energy density of 417 Wh kg −1, and LiCoO 2 ||graphite pouch cells sustain long‐term durability over 5000 cycles. This competitive solvation strategy effectively harmonizes kinetics and interfacial robustness for high‐voltage, fast‐charging DEEs.

title: Ultra‐High Ionic Conductivity Sulfide‐Based Composite Membranes Paired With Stable Interfacial Layer Enables High‐Energy‐Density All‐Solid‐State Batteries
authors: Yang Li, Jiachen Hu, Huan Li, Xu Zhao, Peng Lei, Xiaoxue Zhao et al.
abstract: Intrinsic properties of sulfide solid‐state electrolytes (SEs) are crucial for achieving all‐solid‐state batteries (ASSBs) with high safety and high energy density, yet it is challenging to fabricate high‐performance sulfide SE films in a scalable approach. Furthermore, the inevitable side reactions between sulfide SE and lithium metal anodes exacerbate interfacial incompatibility, causing degradation in the cyclic stability. Here, a high‐performance sulfide SE (Li 5.4 PS 4.4 Cl 0.8 Br 0.8) was selected as the base phase to compensate for the loss of electrochemical performance during the dry film‐forming process. It was then combined with Polytetrafluoroethylene binder to prepare a high‐ionic‐conductivity composite membrane (HICCM). To mitigate side reactions between HICCM and the anode, a LiF‐rich interfacial layer forms in situ on the lithium metal surface, and the assembled symmetric cell achieves a high critical current density of 1.3 mA cm −2 and stable cycling for 2000 h (0.2 mA cm −2). For electrochemical performance, HICCM exhibits fast ion transport kinetics and electrical insulation, allowing the ASSB configured as FeS 2 //HICCM//LiF‐Li to achieve an energy density of 416.5 Wh kg −1 at a high loading of 3.4 mAh cm −2. This work demonstrates that by combining HICCM with a stable interface design, ASSBs can achieve longevity and high cell‐level energy density.

title: N‐Heterocyclic Molecular Additives Enable Solvation and Interfacial Chemistry Regulation for High‐Stability, High‐Rate, and High‐Capacity Lithium Metal Anodes
authors: Fujie Liu, Linglin Xia, Tingting Zhao, Juying Zhou, Jianfang Lu, Cong Liu
abstract: Most electrolyte additives enable long‐term Li plating/stripping at <3 mA cm − 2, non‐applicable to practical Li‐metal batteries (LMBs) operating at ≥5 mA cm − 2 and ≥ 5 mAh cm − 2. Here, we report an interaction chemistry that enables simultaneous solvation and interfacial regulation by exploring a novel N‐heterocyclic molecule (i.e., TPTC)—comprising an N‐heterocyclic core and four pyridine units–as an efficient additive for achieving ultra‐stable Li‐metal anodes under practical conditions. Electron‐rich N atoms in TPTC serve as ion‐dipole interaction sites, inducing competitive coordination that weakens Li + solvation and enhances Li + migration in the bulk electrolyte, which homogenizes Li + concentration near the interface, favoring high‐rate Li deposition. TPTC also adsorbs on Li surface to construct a protective layer with a low interfacial de‐solvation barrier, which–together with low‐barrier Li + transport through heterocyclic cavities–facilitates uniform Li deposition. Meanwhile, electron‐deficient C–H sites in pyridine weakly interact with TFSI −, forming an anion‐rich interfacial region that in situ decomposes into an inorganic‐rich interphase, affording high‐flux Li + transport. This synergy allows stable Li plating/stripping at 10 mA cm −2 /10 mAh cm −2 for 3000 h. Paired with a high‐loading LiFePO 4 cathode (∼15 mg cm −2) and thin Li (∼100 µm), the cell maintains 87.8% capacity after 400 cycles.

title: Operando Mapping of Population Phase Separation and Lithium‐Plating Dynamics in Graphite Electrode Using Optical Microscopy and Microstructure Modeling
authors: Heng Huang, Yang Li, Xuekun Lu, Xinyu Liu, Yang Li, Huanyue Zhang et al.
abstract: The fast‐charging capability of phase‐separating graphite electrodes is largely constrained by heterogeneous reaction kinetics and sluggish mass transport at both the particle and electrode scales, which increase the risk of parasitic lithium plating and associated safety concerns. A deeper mechanistic understanding of the interplay among phase‐separation dynamics, electrode microstructure, and lithium‐plating propensity is therefore essential for guiding the rational design of advanced electrode architectures and fast‐charging protocols. Here, we combine operando optical microscopy with three‐dimensional microstructure‐resolved phase‐field modeling to resolve the interplay between phase separation and lithium plating. Microscopy captures stages evolution, phase mode transitions and structural dynamics across the particle population and at the single‐particle level, which is driven by the slow interfacial reactions. Non‐equilibrium phase‐field simulations elucidate the kinetic control mechanisms governing phase transitions as the current varies. Importantly, a new mechanism of lithium plating associated with interfacial ohmic resistance is identified. Based on these insights, we evaluate particle‐size‐distribution design and use thermal activation as a mechanistic probe to resolve how temperature alters phase‐separation pathways and lithium‐plating behavior. These results may serve as a foundation for improving the physical understanding and driving optimization of fast charging protocols for lithium‐ion batteries.

title: Mechanically‐Driven Reconstruction of Lithium Metal for Stable All‐Solid‐State Batteries
authors: Yujian Sun, Hugo Celio, Arumugam Manthiram
abstract: Dendrite growth at lithium-metal anode remains a critical bottleneck in sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs). Current approaches often rely on alloy anodes that compromise energy density or artificial interlayers, introducing additional processing complexity. Herein, we show that accumulated deformation imposed by repeated folding and rolling mechanically reconstructs commercial Li from surface to bulk, replacing a rough carbonate-rich surface and mixed texture with a refined oxide-passivated surface and a strongly Li(200)-preferred texture. At low and medium folding degrees, surface refinement and renewal of the native passivation layer improve solid-solid contact and interfacial Li-ion transport, but remain insufficient to prevent short circuiting, whereas high-degree reconstruction drives texture homogenization, reduces spatial variations in local interfacial response, and synchronizes Li recession and advancement across the rigid Li | solid-state electrolyte interface. The synchronous interface motion suppresses differential recession and void formation during stripping, while mitigating dendritic Li growth during plating. As a result, Li | LPSCl1.5 | NMC811 full cells achieve 79.3% capacity retention after 1000 cycles at C/2 rate, support 7.4 mA h cm-2 operation with 0.05% decay per cycle, and cycle stably below 0.5 MPa. These findings establish mechanical reconstruction as a direct materials-level strategy for stabilizing Li metal in sulfide-based ASSBs.

title: Bifunctional Additive Enabled Thermoresponsive Electrolytes With Dual‐Mode Manipulation Toward Safe Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Xue Yang, Xiao Hang Guo, Ming Hui Zhang, Yu Hao Huang, Yong Li, Bao Ning Zhu et al.
abstract: Thermal safety issues arising from electrolyte instability at elevated temperatures pose a critical challenge for lithium (Li) metal batteries (LMBs). Thermoresponsive electrolytes offer a promising solution, yet battery systems with high‐rate capability and reliable thermal protection have not been realized. Herein, we introduce a bifunctional LiNO 3 additive into a high‐volume‐fraction vinylene carbonate‐based thermoresponsive electrolyte (HVCE‐N) to enhance the performance of LMBs at room and elevated temperatures. Notably, the introduction of the LiNO 3 additive modifies the solvation structure of Li + and forms a Li 3 N/LiN x O y solid electrolyte interface with high ionic conductivity. Under thermal shock, HVCE‐N undergoes a rapid liquid‐to‐solid phase transition upon free radical polymerization to form a polymer network. More importantly, LiNO 3 can regulate the free radical concentration to control the degree of polymerization, thereby preserving high ion transport capability even after phase transition. As a result, a Li||NCM811 cell based on HVCE‐N exhibits high‐rate performance from 1C to 10C, and stable cycling at 100°C. When subjected to a thermal shock of 200°C, HVCE‐N suppresses thermal runaway for Li||NCM811 pouch cell. This electrolyte design offers a new strategy to develop highly safe LMBs with high‐rate performance.

title: Redirecting Bond Cleavage in Sacrificial Prelithiation via Dual‐Side Separator Engineering for Anode‐Free Lithium Batteries
authors: Junyu Zhang, Xiangrui Tian, Jiawen Tang, Yunsong Li, Wenzhuo Tan, Peiwen Fan et al.
abstract: Anode‐free lithium metal batteries (AFLMBs) promise extreme gravimetric and volumetric energy densities but suffer from irreversible active lithium loss, sluggish desolvation kinetics, and dendritic proliferation. Herein, we report a catalyst‐induced bond‐cleavage redirection concept to unlock efficient sacrificial prelithiation, implemented via a dual‐side functionalized separator. On the cathode side, a 5 µm MoC 1‐x /NC‐0.3Co coating redirects Li 2 C 2 O 4 decomposition from high‐barrier Li–O cleavage to preferential C─C bond scission. Theoretical calculations and operando characterizations confirm this mechanistic shift, lowering the delithiation potential to 3.79 V at 60°C with a 99.5% Li + utilization rate. To safeguard the liberated lithium inventory against depletion, the anode side integrates a PSSLi‐PFPE bilayer. This coating accelerates Li + desolvation and drives the in‐situ construction of a LiF‐rich solid electrolyte interphase, enabling Li symmetric cells cycling for over 1700 h (1.0 mAh cm −2, DOD = 80.7%). Bridging fundamental bond kinetics with practical engineering, the assembled 1.0 Ah anode‐free pouch cell (NCM811||MoC 1‐x /NC‐0.3Co‐LCO/PE/PSSLi‐PFPE||Cu) achieves gravimetric and volumetric energy densities of 458.6 Wh kg −1 and 1005.2 Wh L −1, a power output of 989.1 W kg −1, retaining 80.1% capacity after 100 cycles. This non‐invasive separator strategy provides a unified framework connecting bond kinetics to practical cell manufacturing, charting a feasible avenue for high‐energy AFLMBs.

title: Durable Interphase Incorporating Cross‐Linked Polymer Enables Long‐Calendar‐Life Lithium Metal Batteries
authors: Jia‐lin Li, Jianxin Tian, Qiang Zhang, Yan‐Bin Gao, Dong‐Hao Zhan, Qiankui Zhang et al.
abstract: The practical deployment of lithium (Li) metal batteries is hindered by not only cycle life but also calendar life. The poor calendar life stems from both the repeated reconstruction of the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) during cycles and, particularly, the continuous growth of SEI during storage. Herein, a durable SEI with high mechanical stability against volume fluctuations and superior passivation capability to suppress electrolyte permeation is demonstrated by integrating inorganics and a cross-linked polymer into the SEI. Concretely, a cross-linked polymer with high modulus and low swelling is in-situ incorporated among the inorganics of an anion-derived SEI. The elastic modulus of the SEI is significantly increased from 1.63 to 4.37 GPa, and the compactness of the SEI is also improved to suppress electrolyte permeation. Consequently, the cycle life and calendar life of Li metal coin cells are extended by 73% (from 190 to 329 cycles) and 129% (from 1553 to 3561 h), respectively. Furthermore, a prototype pouch cell (506 Wh kg-1) undergoes 124 cycles. This work establishes an effective strategy that concurrently improves the mechanical and passivation performance of the SEI, tackling the critical challenge of calendar life in Li metal batteries.

title: “Lithium‐Free” Anode Solid‐State Batteries Enabled by 3D Structured Miec Garnet
authors: G. V. Alexander, Aoife Zuercher, Jay Yvonne Easter, Christopher Tang, William Schubert, Jack E. Gritton et al.
abstract: Inhomogeneous lithium nucleation at the current collector‐solid electrolyte interface leads to unstable lithium growth and poor reversibility in “lithium‐free” solid‐state batteries. Here we show that stable lithium formation occurs within a mixed ionic and electronic conducting (MIEC) garnet scaffold. The intrinsic electronic conductivity of the porous framework enables lithium to nucleate uniformly along internal pore surfaces, rapidly forming a conformal lithium coating, thus establishing electronic connectivity at very low lithium volume fraction. This uniform lithium formation dramatically lowers anode impedance, enabling reversible lithium plating and stripping with Coulombic efficiencies of a previously unheard‐of 99.95%. When paired with NMC811 cathodes, bilayer (MIEC(P)‐LLZ(D)) “lithium‐free” full cells exhibit stable, highly reversible cycling at practical current densities, all at room temperature with no applied pressure. The interplay between lithium volume fraction and impedance is quantitatively modeled, transforming the understanding of lithium nucleation in a “lithium‐free” cell from an empirical interface problem to a percolation‐governed transport process, guiding the design of electronically percolating scaffolds for next‐generation solid‐state batteries.

title: A Safety‐Engineered Organic–Inorganic Composite Separator Enabling Fire‐Extinguishing and Dendrite‐Free Lithium Metal Battery Operation
authors: Yichuan Dai, Mingyan Chuai, Xinyu Deng, Zigeng Wu, Yongjie Feng, Dingyi Zhou et al.
abstract: The limited thermal stability, mechanical fragility, and flammability of polyolefin separators impose inherent constraints on the safety and lifespan of lithium metal batteries. Although surface‐coating strategies have been widely explored, single‐component coatings, for example, Al 2 O 3 or polyimide, are unable to simultaneously address dendrite suppression, anti‐thermal shrinkage, and flame retardant. Given these critical challenges, we report a design strategy of multifunctional organic‐inorganic composite separator: (a) an ammonium polyphosphate and poly(acrylic acid) cross‐linked polymer provides intrinsic fire‐retardant behavior and features an electrolyte‐philic characteristic that facilitates Li‐ion transport; (b) a rigid Al 2 O 3 network embedded in the polymer matrix resists thermal shrinkage and blocks dendrite penetration through synergistic SEI protection layers rich in Li 3 N and Li 3 PO 4. Together, these synergistic functions enable Li||Li cells to cycle stably for 2000 h and deliver long‐term stability in LFP||Li full cells (88% capacity retention over 1000 cycles). Moreover, the average heat release rate per unit area (0.04°C min −1 cm −2) of this battery during thermal runaway is markedly suppressed compared to those (0.3°C min −1 cm −2) of batteries using polyolefin separators, pouch cells incorporating this separator consistently exhibit rapid self‐extinguishing behavior during repeated ignition tests. This integrated safety‐centric architecture offers a practical pathway towards intrinsically safe, long‐life lithium metal batteries.
